[Verify live] = a fact that AWS changes often, with an "as of" date: check the AWS page before you rely on it. [Old name] = a name that older material and questions still use. [Beyond the guide] = taught for understanding, not named in the exam guide. [Dates] = a date that matters for the exam.

html:
1What You Will Learn

  • Match AWS WAF, AWS Shield and AWS Firewall Manager to the threat each one stops
  • Tell Amazon GuardDuty, Amazon Inspector, Amazon Macie, Amazon Detective and AWS Security Hub apart
  • Choose among AWS KMS, AWS CloudHSM and AWS Certificate Manager, and say what AWS RAM does
  • Use AWS Trusted Advisor to spot security gaps
  • Know where to find third-party security products and AWS security information

2Block, detect, scan and collect

Running case

Tidewater Prepares for the Sale

  • Tidewater's holiday sale is near, and the shop sits behind a load balancer open to the internet
  • Last year bots and traffic floods slowed the site, and someone tried SQL injection in the search box
  • The team worries about stolen credentials, unpatched servers and customer addresses stored in S3
  • The shop now uses several AWS accounts, and only two people look after security
  • Your job: pick the tools to block, detect, scan and review, and know where to learn more

The Security Toolbox at a Glance

  • Block attacks before they reach the app: AWS WAF, AWS Shield, AWS Firewall Manager
  • Detect and investigate threats: Amazon GuardDuty, Amazon Detective
  • Find weaknesses: Amazon Inspector, Amazon Macie, AWS Trusted Advisor
  • Collect every finding in one place: AWS Security Hub
  • Protect keys, certificates and sharing: AWS KMS, AWS CloudHSM, AWS Certificate Manager, AWS RAM

Exam tip: Each service has one main job; read the verb in the question: block, detect, scan, discover or investigate.

AWS WAF: Filtering Web Requests Old name

  • AWS WAF is a web application firewall: it inspects the HTTP and HTTPS requests sent to your application
  • Attach it to Amazon CloudFront, an Application Load Balancer, Amazon API Gateway REST APIs, AWS AppSync and other supported resources
  • Rules sit in a web ACL (access control list; the new console says protection pack); a rule can allow, block, count or ask for a CAPTCHA
  • Match IP addresses, headers and query strings; a rate-based rule limits requests that arrive too fast
  • Managed rule groups block common attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting

Exam tip: Web exploits and bad bots at the application layer: AWS WAF.

AWS Shield: Standard and Advanced [Verify live]

Shield Standard Shield Advanced
Cost Automatic, no extra charge Paid subscription
Defends against Common network and transport layer DDoS attacks Expanded protection, plus automatic layer 7 mitigation with AWS WAF
Resources All customers; strongest for Route 53, CloudFront, Global Accelerator Resources you add: CloudFront, Route 53 zones, Global Accelerator, Elastic IPs, load balancers
Extras Nothing to set up Shield Response Team, cost protection as credits, health-based detection
  • A DDoS attack floods a target from many systems so real users cannot get in
  • As of 4 November 2026: the Response Team needs a paid support plan, and plan names are changing (Module 14)

Exam tip: Free and automatic: Standard. Response team and cost protection: Advanced.

AWS Firewall Manager: One Policy, Many Accounts

  • AWS Firewall Manager sets protections up once and applies them across accounts and resources in AWS Organizations
  • It manages AWS WAF, AWS Shield Advanced, security groups and network ACLs, AWS Network Firewall and Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall
  • Scope a policy to all resources of a type or to resources with specific tags
  • New accounts and resources are protected automatically
  • You pay for the underlying services, such as AWS WAF and AWS Config

Exam tip: One place to manage firewall rules for many accounts: Firewall Manager.

Amazon GuardDuty: Threat Detection

  • Amazon GuardDuty is threat detection: it watches your account for suspicious activity continuously
  • Once on, it analyzes CloudTrail management events, VPC flow logs and DNS logs
  • It uses threat intelligence (known malicious IP addresses and domains) and machine learning
  • It finds things like compromised credentials, cryptomining and malware
  • Optional protection plans add sources such as S3, EKS, RDS logins, Lambda, malware scanning and runtime monitoring
  • Findings go to Security Hub, Detective and EventBridge; new accounts get a 30-day free trial

Exam tip: Suspicious activity and compromised credentials: GuardDuty.

Amazon Inspector: Finding Weaknesses

  • Amazon Inspector is vulnerability management: it looks for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure
  • It scans Amazon EC2 instances, container images in Amazon ECR and AWS Lambda functions
  • Scanning is automatic and continuous; it rescans when you install a package, apply a patch or a new CVE is published
  • Each finding names the resource and suggests a fix, with a risk score adjusted to your environment
  • Findings flow to EventBridge and Security Hub
  • Remember: GuardDuty asks "what is happening?"; Inspector asks "what could be exploited?"

Exam tip: Known vulnerabilities (CVEs) on instances, images or functions: Inspector.

Amazon Macie: Sensitive Data in S3

  • Amazon Macie finds sensitive data in Amazon S3 using machine learning and pattern matching
  • It detects personally identifiable information (PII), financial information and credentials; you can add custom data identifiers
  • It keeps an inventory of your S3 buckets and flags risks, such as a bucket that becomes publicly accessible
  • Automated discovery samples your buckets; discovery jobs go deeper, once or on a schedule
  • Findings go to EventBridge and Security Hub; new accounts get a 30-day free trial

Exam tip: Sensitive data, such as PII, stored in S3: Macie.

Amazon Detective: Finding the Root Cause

  • Amazon Detective helps you investigate a security finding and find its root cause
  • It collects CloudTrail logs, VPC flow logs and GuardDuty findings automatically
  • It builds a behavior graph with visual summaries over time, keeping up to a year of history
  • It answers questions such as "is this an unusual API call for this role?"
  • You can jump from a GuardDuty finding straight into Detective
  • Remember: GuardDuty detects; Detective investigates

Exam tip: Detect: GuardDuty. Investigate the root cause: Detective.

AWS Security Hub: One View of Findings Old name [Verify live]

  • AWS Security Hub gives one view of your security state across accounts, AWS services and partner products
  • It receives findings from GuardDuty, Inspector and Macie
  • It also checks your setup against standards: AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, CIS, PCI DSS and NIST
  • Automation rules and EventBridge can act on findings
  • Most checks need AWS Config recording turned on
  • As of 4 November 2026: the documentation names the service AWS Security Hub CSPM; the exam may say Security Hub

Exam tip: One place to see findings and standards checks from many services: Security Hub.

3Keys, reviews, resources and practice

Keys and Certificates: KMS, CloudHSM and ACM

Service What it does Choose it when
AWS KMS Creates and controls the keys that encrypt and sign your data; keys sit in FIPS 140-3 Level 3 hardware security modules; key policies control access You want a managed key service that works with AWS services
AWS CloudHSM Dedicated, single-tenant hardware security modules in your VPC; you control keys, algorithms and users Rules demand full control of the HSMs, and you accept more responsibility
AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) Creates, stores and renews public and private SSL/TLS certificates for integrated services You need HTTPS on a load balancer or CloudFront
  • ACM adds no charge for certificates; you pay for the resources that use them

Exam tip: Managed keys: KMS. Your own dedicated hardware: CloudHSM. Website certificates: ACM.

AWS Resource Access Manager: Share, Don't Copy

  • AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) lets you share your resources with other AWS accounts, with an organization or organizational unit, and, for some types, with IAM roles and users
  • Create a resource once, then share it, instead of building a copy in every account
  • A shared resource looks native in the other account: a shared VPC subnet appears in the VPC console
  • The owner keeps ownership; a managed permission on the resource share sets what others may do, and their IAM policies and SCPs still apply
  • No additional charge for AWS RAM; you pay for the shared resource itself

Exam tip: Share a resource with other accounts without duplicating it: AWS RAM.

AWS Trusted Advisor: Security Checks Old name [Verify live]

  • AWS Trusted Advisor inspects your account and recommends ways to save money, improve performance and availability, and close security gaps
  • Every account gets the service limits checks and core security checks: S3 bucket permissions, security groups with unrestricted ports, MFA on the root account, and public EBS and RDS snapshots
  • The full set of checks and the API need a paid support plan
  • As of 4 November 2026: the full set comes with Business Support+, Enterprise Support or Unified Operations; older material says Business or Enterprise Support

Exam tip: A quick review for security gaps: Trusted Advisor; the full set needs a paid plan.

AWS Marketplace: Third-Party Security Products

  • AWS Marketplace is a curated digital catalog to find, test, buy and deploy third-party software
  • Security listings come from independent software vendors in areas such as application security, endpoint security, identity and access control, SIEM, WAF and edge security and managed security services
  • Use it for a product your team already knows, or one AWS does not offer as a service
  • Managed rules for AWS WAF can also come from Marketplace sellers
  • Remember: you still configure and operate what you deploy

Exam tip: A third-party security product, bought and deployed on AWS: AWS Marketplace.

Where to Find Security Information [Verify live]

Resource What you find there
AWS Security Blog How-to guides, announcements and compliance news
AWS Knowledge Center Answers to common AWS questions, hosted with AWS re:Post
AWS re:Post Community questions and answers
AWS Security Center The exam guide's name; the AWS cloud security pages gather services, learning, compliance, whitepapers and reference architecture
Report a problem Pages to report vulnerabilities and suspicious emails
  • As of 4 November 2026: no page is titled exactly "AWS Security Center"; the cloud security pages play that role

Exam tip: Learn from the Security Blog and Knowledge Center; get AWS's compliance reports from AWS Artifact.

What the Exam Asks: Security Services

  • Web attack or flood: WAF filters requests; Shield absorbs DDoS attacks
  • Many accounts, one policy: Firewall Manager
  • Detect or scan: GuardDuty detects threats; Inspector finds vulnerabilities
  • Discover or investigate: Macie finds PII in S3; Detective finds the root cause
  • See everything together: Security Hub
  • Keys, hardware or certificates: KMS, CloudHSM, ACM
  • Review or buy: Trusted Advisor reviews; Marketplace sells third-party products

Exam tip: Name the verb first, then the service.

Design Check: Tidewater's Security Plan

Tidewater's worry Choose
SQL injection and bad bots at the load balancer AWS WAF with managed rule groups and a rate-based rule
Traffic floods during the sale Shield Standard (automatic); Shield Advanced for the most critical sites
The same web rules in every account, including new ones AWS Firewall Manager
Stolen credentials or cryptomining GuardDuty, then Detective to find the root cause
Unpatched servers and container images Amazon Inspector
Customer addresses stored in S3 Amazon Macie
One place for every finding AWS Security Hub
Open ports and public buckets, found quickly AWS Trusted Advisor
  • Cover the right column, answer each row yourself, then compare

4Exam Q&A

4.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer; some ask for two)

S1Tidewater's shop sits behind an Application Load Balancer, and attackers are sending SQL injection strings in search requests. Which service can block these requests before they reach the application?

  • AAWS Shield Standard, which is switched on automatically
  • BAmazon Inspector, which scans the web servers for weaknesses
  • CAmazon GuardDuty, which analyzes logs to detect threats
  • DAWS WAF, with a web ACL attached to the load balancer
Show the answer

Answer: D. AWS WAF inspects HTTP and HTTPS requests and blocks patterns such as SQL injection through rules and managed rule groups. Shield Standard defends against network and transport layer floods, Inspector finds vulnerabilities and GuardDuty detects threats, but none of them filters web requests.

S2Which service continuously analyzes AWS CloudTrail events, VPC flow logs and DNS logs, using threat intelligence and machine learning, to detect suspicious activity such as cryptomining or compromised credentials?

  • AAmazon GuardDuty
  • BAmazon Inspector
  • CAmazon Macie
  • DAWS Trusted Advisor
Show the answer

Answer: A. GuardDuty is the threat detection service that watches those data sources and reports findings. Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities, Macie discovers sensitive data in Amazon S3, and Trusted Advisor recommends improvements from its checks.

S3Which TWO benefits come with an AWS Shield Advanced subscription but not with AWS Shield Standard? (Select TWO.)

  • AProtection that is applied automatically at no extra charge
  • BAccess to the Shield Response Team during a DDoS attack
  • CDefense against common network and transport layer attacks
  • DCost protection, given as service credits after an attack
  • EScans of container images for software vulnerabilities
Show the answer

Answer: B, D. Shield Advanced adds access to the Shield Response Team, which also needs a paid support plan, and cost protection in the form of service credits. Automatic, no-charge protection against common network and transport layer attacks is what Shield Standard already provides, and container image scanning is Amazon Inspector.

S4Tidewater now runs thirty accounts in AWS Organizations. The security team wants the same AWS WAF rules applied in every account, including accounts created later, from one place. Which service should it use?

  • AAWS Security Hub, to collect findings from every account
  • BAmazon GuardDuty, with a delegated administrator account
  • CAWS Firewall Manager, with a policy for the organization
  • DAWS Shield Standard, which is enabled in each account
Show the answer

Answer: C. Firewall Manager applies AWS WAF rules and other protections across accounts in an organization and covers new accounts and resources automatically. Security Hub collects findings, GuardDuty detects threats, and Shield Standard is automatic but has no rules to manage.

S5A new administrator wants a quick review of the account for security gaps, such as a publicly accessible Amazon S3 bucket, security group ports left open and a root user without MFA. Which AWS tool gives these recommendations?

  • AAWS Artifact
  • BAWS Trusted Advisor
  • CAmazon Inspector
  • DAWS Marketplace
Show the answer

Answer: B. Trusted Advisor inspects the account and recommends fixes, and its core security checks include bucket permissions, unrestricted security group ports and MFA on the root account. Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities and network exposure, Artifact provides compliance reports and Marketplace sells third-party software.

S6Tidewater wants a third-party endpoint protection product that AWS does not offer as a service. Where can it find, buy and deploy such security software on AWS?

  • AAWS Marketplace, which lists software from independent vendors
  • BThe AWS Security Blog, which publishes security how-to posts
  • CThe AWS Knowledge Center, which answers common questions
  • DAWS Artifact, which provides compliance reports and agreements
Show the answer

Answer: A. AWS Marketplace is the catalog for finding, testing, buying and deploying third-party software, including security products. The Security Blog and Knowledge Center are places to learn, and Artifact provides AWS's own compliance reports and agreements.

5Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Block AWS WAF filters web requests, Shield defends against DDoS, Firewall Manager applies protections across accounts
Detect and investigate GuardDuty finds threats, Detective finds the root cause
Find weaknesses Inspector scans for vulnerabilities, Macie finds sensitive data in S3, Trusted Advisor checks for gaps
Collect Security Hub brings findings and standards checks together
Protect KMS manages keys, CloudHSM gives dedicated hardware, ACM manages certificates, RAM shares resources
Learn and buy Marketplace for third-party products; Security Blog, Knowledge Center and AWS cloud security pages for information
